institution: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
title: A fossil fish from the Santana Formation
dateKind: Date range of the geological formation in the record. The collecting entry is 1907.
medium: Fossil fish, catalogued as Aspidorhynchus comptoni
observation: The catalogue places this specimen in the Santana Formation, and the collecting entry says 1907. The photograph is a separate view, credited to Holly Little.
limit: The catalogue gives a geological period and a collection year. The visible slab alone does not locate a layer within the formation.
action: The museum’s image shows one face of the slab. This padded practice cradle can turn. The age of the formation and the collecting year have separate slips.
result: The fossil-bearing face is clear from one side. The collecting year can stay with the catalogue slip while the formation stays beside the slab.
alt: Light stone with a fossil fish and a scale strip at the top of the image.
tryAction: Turn the cradle and tuck the collecting slip under the scale
fieldAction: Set the faced-up cradle beside the collector’s loose slip
deskAction: File the formation, collection and photograph tabs separately
fieldReply: I can turn this practice cradle back without turning the collection slip over. Next visitor can check the fossil-bearing side from here.
deskReply: Three pockets. Next winter, I can trace the date someone recovered the fossil and still find the person who made the photograph.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
title: Raninoides fossil, Zulia
dateKind: Geological epoch. The collecting record dates the recovery to November 1923.
place: Zulia, Venezuela. Pauji Shale as abbreviated in the catalogue.
medium: Fossil crab, catalogued to the genus Raninoides
observation: The catalogue identifies the genus and the Eocene age of the recorded formation. Its collecting record is November 1923.
limit: The record names a genus. It leaves the species unresolved, and the geological epoch is a separate date from field collection.
action: The genus tab and the dated tabs share a narrow strip. The tab for November 1923 is long enough to hide the fossil’s geological age.
result: The genus can be read with the epoch in one view and the collecting month in its own pocket.
alt: Two rounded stone faces beside a small catalogue slip and a scale.
tryAction: Raise the Eocene tab and lower the recovery tab
fieldAction: Leave the species slot open on the teaching frame
deskAction: File the accession and photograph with the species slot still open
fieldReply: One name I can show. One I can leave open. I’ll put the movable species tab by the rail for a later specialist.
deskReply: The source tray leaves a space after the genus. I’ll file the photographer and accession beside it so the next person can return to this record.

title: A jaw fragment catalogued as Eocaiman
dateKind: Geological epoch of the lower Villavieja Formation. The collecting entry gives 1965.
place: Huila Department, Colombia. Lower Villavieja Formation.
observation: The Yale Peabody record identifies this as a mandible fragment and places it in the lower Villavieja Formation. The image concerns this exact catalogue number.
limit: The fragment does not resolve the size of the entire animal. The specimen record names a genus and gives the epoch separately from collection.
action: The jaw exercise has a fragment and a longer imagined outline. The scale on the catalogue image applies to the photographed fragment.
result: The outline fits the fragment window. The vacant extension stays unmeasured and the note stays about a jaw fragment.
alt: A small brown jaw fragment with a label and a ten-centimetre scale bar.
tryAction: Slide the clear outline back to the surviving fragment
fieldAction: Fit the movable outline around the fragment alone
deskAction: File the source outline and keep the conjectured extension on a separate sheet
fieldReply: The frame stops where the fragment stops. I’ll leave the rest of the rack bare so the next visitor can try the fit from the beginning.
deskReply: The fragment drawing and the trial extension can go in different sleeves. Someone can borrow the source outline without copying the other one.

title: Approach to Montevideo, Uruguay
place: Montevideo, Uruguay, as named in the title.
observation: The Met dates this watercolor over graphite to 1832 and attributes it to Conrad Martens. The sheet offers one drawn approach to Montevideo.
limit: The drawing records a view within its frame. It does not supply a complete route survey or verify present access.
action: A route line runs from the practice drawing onto blank paper. You can move the viewfinder to the actual boundary of the view.
result: The frame shows the visible shore. The route line ends where the drawing does.
alt: Watercolor view with buildings on a headland and water under a cloudy sky.
tryAction: Slide the viewfinder to the paper edge and stop the route line there
fieldAction: Lay the edge of the frame over the place where the route line stops
deskAction: File the bounded view beside the artist, place and date
fieldReply: I can show a visitor where the paper ends before we talk about where a boat could go. Here, this edge stays up.
deskReply: The next reader can call up the same sheet by artist, named place and date. I’ll keep those fields with the view edge.

title: A Brazilian Landscape
place: Brazil is the setting named by the Met. The painter was Dutch.
observation: The Met records an oil painting on wood by Frans Post, dated 1650. The painting presents a view of Brazil as organised by the painter.
limit: The painting’s arrangement supports visual interpretation. The scene cannot confirm the viewpoints or experiences of people represented in it.
action: A mask can isolate a detail in the painted foreground. The date tab belongs to the picture. The open pocket is for a source outside the painting.
result: The frame isolates a visible feature, and the caption keeps the picture’s date apart from an imagined date for the scene.
alt: Painted view with a tree at the right and small figures in the foreground.
tryAction: Frame the foreground and pull out the painting’s date tab
fieldAction: Try the foreground frame with one reader at a time
deskAction: File the artist and date with an open pocket for another account
fieldReply: I can move the mask with a reader who points to a different detail. The picture’s date still belongs to the picture.
deskReply: I’ll clip the painting record and leave a separate open pocket for another account. A person in a picture can’t tell me what they thought from here.

title: Infernal Rock, Chincha Islands
dateKind: Estimated date of the albumen print, about 1870.
place: Chincha Islands, Peru, as named in the catalogue title.
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
observation: The Met catalogues this as an albumen silver print from a glass negative, attributed to an unknown maker and dated about 1870. Its image measures 18.4 × 25.3 cm.
limit: The print frames one view. It leaves activity beyond the frame and the photographer’s position open.
action: The small mask for the practice photograph can hide the edge of the print. The date and the print process travel on their own tab.
result: The mask shows where the view stops. The photograph stays linked to its own print process and approximate date.
alt: A brown-toned photograph of a rock arch surrounded by water.
tryAction: Align the paper mask with the edge of the print exercise
fieldAction: Leave an edge visible in the small glance window
deskAction: File the dated print with its medium and maker field
fieldReply: That lip makes the edge easy to feel on our little teaching frame. I’ll leave the window set there for the next visitor.
deskReply: I’ll keep the approximate print date, print process and the maker field on this slip. The catalogue has no named maker to copy into it.

title: Pair of Stirrups from Argentina
dateKind: Century of making assigned by the catalogue, nineteenth century.
place: Argentina, as catalogued by the Met.
observation: The Met lists the iron-alloy pair with equal recorded heights (18.4 cm). It gives separate masses of 368.5 g and 365.7 g.
limit: The measurements describe the two catalogued pieces. They do not give a named rider’s experience or show how either was made.
action: Two practice fittings share a height stop. Each sits on the balance by itself. The catalogue gives two different masses for the pair.
result: Both fit the height stop. The balance keeps two separate mass entries.
alt: Two iron-alloy stirrups with a ribbed lower cage, photographed obliquely.
tryAction: Set one height stop and weigh each fitting separately
fieldAction: Let the next visitor use the stop and read both mass slips
deskAction: Keep each number with its mass slip under the pair entry
fieldReply: One stop. Two slips. The next visitor can try the same fit twice before we swap places at the balance.
deskReply: I can look up either number under the pair entry. I’ll fasten the mass slips below their matching numbers.

title: Warp Patterned Cloth from Salinas
dateKind: Catalogue dates the making to the late nineteenth century.
observation: The Cleveland Museum lists a wool cloth dated to the late nineteenth century and measures it at 110.5 × 101.6 cm overall.
limit: The measured size applies to this cloth. The entry leaves the maker and exact everyday use unstated.
action: The plain practice frame has a long and a short stop. Each has a named axis. Turning the frame will move the stops along with it.
result: The long and short stops fit the measurement. No working instruction for the cloth’s own pattern is assumed.
alt: A rectangular woven cloth with broad dark and red bands.
tryAction: Slide the long and short stops into the marked slots
fieldAction: Leave the two named stops ready for the next reader
deskAction: File both measured axes, the place and the making period
fieldReply: I’ll keep both stop names where a shorter visitor can read them. A turn of the frame won’t quietly swap the two measured sides.
deskReply: The next reader can find Salinas and the period with both dimensions. I’ll keep those together and leave the maker field as the catalogue gives it.

title: Wool and Jute Belt from Ecuador
dateKind: Catalogue’s approximate date of making. It gives c. 1900s and describes twentieth-century Ecuador.
place: Ecuador, as catalogued by the Cleveland Museum.
medium: Wool and jute, warp face in extended tabby
observation: This specific belt contains wool and jute. Its overall length and width in the catalogue are 185.4 cm and 5.1 cm.
limit: The public provenance lists a purchase from Paul Young without a date. The overall measurements do not say how a particular wearer fitted the belt.
action: The model’s long bar opens into the aisle. Its short width guide can lift free without extending the bar.
result: The band reaches the catalogue length in the model. The two marked sides describe different dimensions.
alt: A long narrow woven belt shown extended vertically.
frame: the length bar and short guide
tryAction: Set the short width guide and unroll the band to the length mark
fieldAction: Leave the short guide out before the long bar extends
deskAction: File the purchase entry and making date on different lines
fieldReply: I’ll keep the little guide out. A visitor can use it without opening the long bar into the path.
deskReply: The receipt says from whom the museum purchased the belt. It gives no date. I’ll file that receipt in its own pocket.
